title: The medieval church
premise: The surviving record of the church from about AD 500 to 1350 is mostly written from the top, by popes, councils, kings and bishops, so a reader has to ask of each sentence whether it says what someone wanted or what people did.
question: Who wrote this down, and how far did it reach?
outcomes: Tell what a council, pope or king decreed from what the record shows happened next.
Keep a baptised ruler apart from a believing people, and say who wrote the story and how long after.
Follow how popes and kings each claimed the upper hand, and name the event that tested the claim.
Read a disputed question in its own five moves, and say what a thirteenth-century student had to do to reach it.
Walk a parish church from gate to altar, naming the rule at each step and how little shows whether it was kept.

boundaries.in: About AD 500 to 1350 in the Latin West: the conversion of northern Europe, popes and kings, the universities and the method of the schools as an institution, and ordinary parish life.
out: The split between East and West, and the conversions of Bulgaria and Kyiv: planned study Traditions: shared roots & divisions.
Monastic spirituality and the rule of life: planned study The church, worship & the good life. Monks appear here only as missionaries and scholars.
How medieval readers read the Bible, including the four senses: How the church has read the Bible.
Wycliffe, the Lollards, Hus and the Reformation: the Reformation outline and planned study Reform, renewal & revival.
The first Christian generations, to about AD 300: planned study of that name.
Jews and Christians, including the council's rules on Jews and the disputations: planned study Jews and Christians across the centuries.

The crusades to the Holy Land and the inquisition have no study of their own yet. The Baltic wars appear here only as a way northern Europe was made Christian, and the Toulouse ruling only as the Bible claim requires. They are real and large, and this page does not cover them.
What each great thinker taught: planned study Works that shaped Christianity. Aquinas appears here for the form of his argument, not for his system.
What councils defined as doctrine: planned study Creeds & councils. The Fourth Lateran Council appears here for what it asked of priests and parishes.
What worship and the sacraments meant to those who took part: the planned part Worship & spiritual life. The parish section reports rules and records only.

fields.name: Mission
fields.note: Who was baptised, and what changed

fields.name: Parish
fields.note: What priests and people were told

pairs.head: Keep the temple. Break the idol.

declared.who: Pope Gregory I, to Abbot Mellitus, going to Kent
declared.quote: the temples of the idols in that nation ought not to be destroyed; but let the idols that are in them be destroyed

followed.who: King Rædwald of the East Angles, as Bede tells it
followed.quote: in the same temple he had an altar to sacrifice to Christ, and another small one to offer victims to devils

pairs.evidence: Gregory's letter survives in Bede, book 1 chapter 30. It argues that people rise “by degrees or steps, and not by leaps”. Bede, book 2 chapter 15, says Rædwald was baptised in Kent and then kept two altars in one temple, and that a later king had seen that temple as a boy.
pairs.inference: This study sets the two side by side because they show the same ground from two ends. A slow change can look patient from Rome and like two altars from East Anglia.
pairs.limit: Rædwald's temple is not a result of Gregory's letter: nothing connects them, so the thread here is dashed. Bede gives no year for it, so the range runs from about the time of his baptism to his death. Bede wrote over a century later and disapproved.

pairs.head: Baptism or death. Then revolt.

declared.quote: shall have scorned to come to baptism and shall have wished to remain a pagan, let him be punished by death

followed.who: The same king, and the Saxons
followed.what: Wars and risings run on to 804. In 797 Charlemagne himself eases the special laws.

pairs.evidence: The capitulary's eighth chapter makes refusing baptism a capital crime, and its fourteenth lets a secret offender who confesses to a priest escape death. Wars with risings ran from 772 to 804. In 797 Charlemagne eased the special laws. Alcuin, at his court, wrote about 796 that a person can be drawn into the faith, not forced.
pairs.inference: The law shows what the conqueror wanted. The easing and the long wars suggest it did not get it by that road. This study does not claim Alcuin's letter caused the change.
pairs.limit: A law does not record how often it was used. The law's date is itself a range here, and the English comes from a 1900 translation. The record of the Saxons' own thinking is close to nil: nearly everything comes from the Frankish side.

pairs.head: One law. Sacrifice in secret.

declared.who: The Icelandic assembly, on the law-speaker's ruling
declared.quote: all people had to be Christian and accept baptism

followed.who: The same ruling, and its exceptions
followed.quote: People had to make sacrifices in secret, if they wanted to avoid three-year outlawry

pairs.evidence: Ari Thorgilsson, writing over a century later, says the ruling kept exposing infants and eating horse-meat as they were, and allowed sacrifice in private unless there were witnesses. He adds that “a few years later, that heathen practice was also taken away”.
pairs.inference: Here baptism arrived as a settlement between factions, to keep one law in one land. The exceptions name what the settlement left alone.
pairs.limit: Ari is the earliest account and writes from a Christian bishop's world. He gives no year for the later change, so the range drawn here is this study's and only says “a few years”. The English is a volunteer translation on Wikisource.

pairs.head: May depose emperors. Dies in exile.

declared.who: The Dictates of the Pope, in Gregory VII's register
declared.quote: That it may be permitted to him to depose emperors.

followed.what: Henry stands a penitent at Canossa in 1077, and enters Rome in 1084. Gregory leaves with the Normans and dies at Salerno in 1085.

pairs.evidence: The list also says the pope “may be judged by no one”. Gregory deposed Henry in 1076. In January 1077 Henry stood as a penitent at the gate of Canossa and was absolved. In March 1084 Henry entered Rome, and an opposing pope crowned him emperor. Gregory left with the Normans who rescued him, and died at Salerno in May 1085.
pairs.inference: Each side had a real weapon. Gregory could strip a king of his princes' loyalty for a time, and Henry could take Rome. The claim held on parchment, and was only partly true on the road to Salerno.
pairs.limit: Some scholars date the list's compiling later than 1075, and it may not be Gregory's own writing. Whether Canossa was a king's humiliation or his clever escape is argued: it restored him to the church and undercut the princes against him. This study knows that argument through reference articles and names no side.

pairs.head: A king's rules. A dead archbishop.

declared.who: Henry II of England, the Constitutions of Clarendon
declared.what: Sixteen articles curb church courts and appeals to Rome.

followed.who: Thomas Becket, and Henry at Avranches
followed.what: Becket opposes them and is killed in his cathedral in 1170. At Avranches in 1172 Henry gives up the customs the church objected to.

pairs.evidence: Popes were not the only ones to write rules. Henry's sixteen articles curbed church courts and appeals to Rome. Archbishop Becket opposed them and was killed in his cathedral in 1170. At Avranches in 1172 Henry was cleared of guilt, agreed to allow appeals to Rome and gave up the customs the church objected to.
pairs.inference: A paper can fail from the king's side as well. This pair is here so that the pattern is not read as being only about popes.
pairs.limit: This study read about these through reference articles, not the chroniclers. How far Henry's concessions changed daily practice in English courts is not something those articles settle.

pairs.head: Every creature subject. Then Anagni.

declared.who: Pope Boniface VIII, the bull Unam Sanctam
declared.quote: it is absolutely necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff

followed.who: Philip IV's men, and the popes after
followed.what: In 1303 the French king's adviser and Sciarra Colonna seize the pope at Anagni. In 1309 the papal court moves to Avignon.

pairs.evidence: In 1303 the French king's adviser Nogaret and Sciarra Colonna seized the pope at Anagni. The townspeople freed him after about three days, and he died in Rome that October. In 1309 the papal court moved to Avignon, where seven popes in turn resided until 1376.
pairs.inference: The highest claim in this period's record and one of its plainest defeats fall a year apart. So how high a claim is written does not show how far it reached.
pairs.limit: Avignon was not French land at the time, and how far those popes were the crown's men is argued, so “defeat” describes Anagni better than Avignon. The slap of Anagni is a legend.

pairs.head: Not to be read. Then required.

declared.who: Cardinal Robert de Courçon, statutes for the masters at Paris
declared.quote: The books of Aristotle on Metaphysics or Natural Philosophy, or the abridgements of these works, are not to be read

followed.who: Pope Gregory IX, and the Paris masters of arts
followed.what: In 1231 the ban is kept only until the books are cleared of error. In 1255 the masters of arts set the Physics and the Metaphysics on their list.

pairs.evidence: In 1231 Gregory IX kept the ban only until the books had been examined and cleared of error. In 1255 the masters of arts laid down how long a master must take over a list of texts, and it includes the Physics and the Metaphysics.
pairs.inference: Here the rule went one way and the school went the other, within forty years. The later statute treats the once-forbidden books as ordinary teaching.
pairs.limit: The ban bound Paris only, and concerned lecturing: it did not stop a private reader. The bishop of Paris condemned 219 theses in 1277, so the argument over what Aristotle allowed did not end in 1255.

pairs.head: A master in every cathedral. Not observed.

declared.who: The Third Lateran Council, as the Fourth reports it
declared.quote: in every cathedral church a suitable benefice be assigned to a master

followed.who: The Fourth Lateran Council, on the same rule
followed.quote: But, since in many churches this is not observed

pairs.evidence: Canon 11 of 1215 quotes the older rule, says it is not being kept in many churches, confirms it, and widens it to other churches with the means, adding a theologian at each metropolitan church.
pairs.inference: This is the rare case where the record says so itself. A council is the witness that its own earlier rule had not reached.
pairs.limit: “Many churches” is the council's own phrase, with no count. The canon does not say which churches kept the rule, or how many.

pairs.head: Prepare your priests. “Pater, for He governeth all things.”

declared.quote: If in the future they presume to ordain ignorant and unformed men

followed.who: The dean of Salisbury's visit to Sonning, and the curate Simon
followed.quote: He knew not the case of Te, nor by what word it was governed

pairs.evidence: Seven years after the canon, a dean examined a curate who had been made priest about four years earlier, so after it. Simon was found unable to understand the Gospel he read, could not parse the opening words of the prayer of the Mass, and thought it indecent to be examined at all. The clerk's note ends: “He is amply illiterate.”
pairs.inference: A rule made in Rome in 1215 had not settled who stood at the altar in a Berkshire village in 1222. Latin the priest could say and could not follow is a real gap between the two.
pairs.limit: One man is not a clergy. Records of this kind exist to find faults, so they do not show the priests who were found adequate. The same visit is the evidence that someone was checking.

pairs.head: Live chastely. “Ill-famed of incontinence.”

declared.quote: let all strive to live chastely and virtuously, particularly those in sacred orders

followed.who: Archbishop Odo Rigaud, visiting his own cathedral at Rouen
followed.quote: many other of the statutes written on the board in the vestry are not kept

pairs.evidence: Odo's register names canons of Rouen as ill-famed of incontinence, tavern-going, dicing and trading, and says the clergy talk during the service. He sets a date for correction.
pairs.inference: Clergy conduct remained a live problem a generation on, at the head of a province and not only in remote villages. It also shows the reformers at work: Odo wrote down what he found and demanded it be fixed.
pairs.limit: “Ill-famed” means reported, not proved. This is one cathedral on one day, chosen here because its English is available. It is a cathedral, placed under Parish because the same rules reach down to the clergy of every parish.

pairs.head: Confess each year. Teach them what to confess.

declared.quote: All the faithful of both sexes shall after they have reached the age of discretion faithfully confess all their sins at least once a year

followed.who: Archbishop John Pecham's council at Lambeth
followed.what: English priests are told to explain the faith to their people, in their own tongue, four times a year.

pairs.evidence: Sixty-six years on, Pecham's council told English priests to explain to their people, in their own tongue, four times a year, the articles of faith, the commandments, the works of mercy, the deadly sins, the virtues and the sacraments. The decree is known by its opening words, Ignorantia sacerdotum: the ignorance of priests.
pairs.inference: A yearly duty needs a people who know what it asks. The 1281 programme reads as the long second half of the 1215 rule, and shows the church taking the people's ignorance seriously.
pairs.limit: A decree that opens by naming ignorance is a reformer's opening, not a survey. Whether priests did teach four times a year is not known from it. This study read reports of the decree and not its Latin.

stations.name: The Franks
stations.head: “Burn what you worshipped.”
stations.text: King Clovis asks for baptism first, and the bishop tells him: “worship what you burned; burn what you worshipped.” Clovis took the Catholic faith where most Germanic rulers held the Arian one, and it bound the Franks to the bishops of Gaul.
stations.limit: Gregory writes about ninety years on, and casts Clovis as “another Constantine”. Modern dates for the baptism range over several years.

stations.name: Kent
stations.head: “Voluntary, not by compulsion.”
stations.text: Gregory sends Augustine and his monks to King Æthelberht. Bede says the king favoured those who believed but “compelled none”, having learned “that the service of Christ ought to be voluntary, not by compulsion”.
stations.limit: Bede writes over 130 years later, wanting this as a model. How many in Kent were baptised, and how soon, is not a number anyone can give.

stations.name: Northumbria
stations.head: A sparrow through the hall.
stations.text: King Edwin puts the matter to his council. One chief man likens this life to “the swift flight of a sparrow through the room wherein you sit at supper in winter”, and says that if the new teaching holds something more certain, it should be followed. Edwin is baptised at York.
stations.limit: Bede composes the speech a century on. It shows what he thought a good reason for conversion was, and may be close to nothing that was said in the hall.

stations.name: Hesse
stations.head: He cut down the oak.
stations.text: Boniface, an English monk, fells a tree sacred to the people of Hesse with a crowd of them looking on, and builds a chapel from its timber. He was killed in Frisia in 754, still at the mission as an old man.
stations.limit: Willibald wrote a saint's life, within living memory. The date is a reconstruction, the tree's god is named in Latin dress, and the Life itself says some kept sacrificing, in secret and in the open.

stations.name: Saxony
stations.head: Drawn, and not forced.
stations.text: Thirty-two years of campaigns and risings ended with Saxony inside the Frankish realm. Alcuin wrote about 796: “Attrahi poterit homo in fidem, non cogi”: a person can be drawn into the faith, not forced. Baptism could be forced, he says, and it would do nothing for faith.
stations.limit: Alcuin in the same breath excepts infants, who may be saved by others' confession, so he is not arguing for believer's baptism. A modern paper argues he did not object to the armies themselves: this study knows it only through a listing.

stations.name: Denmark
stations.head: “And made the Danes Christian.”
stations.text: King Harald raises a stone for his parents and adds his own record: he “won for himself all of Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian”. Ansgar had preached in Denmark over a century before, with little that lasted.
stations.limit: This is a boast in the king's own voice, cut in granite while he lived. It records what he wished to be known for, and the Danes left no reply.

stations.name: Poland
stations.head: A duke and his court.
stations.text: Duke Mieszko I is baptised with much of his court, and Poland's millennium was counted from it in 1966. His wife, Dobrawa of Bohemia, is often credited with a large part in it. Spreading it through the land took far longer.
stations.limit: Where it happened is disputed, with Poznań and Gniezno the likeliest, so the mark here is hollow: it stands for the country, not a known spot. The year is firmer than the place. The date written here for the first chronicler is approximate.

stations.name: Iceland
stations.head: One law, to keep the peace.
stations.text: The two parties at the assembly were close to fighting. The law-speaker Thorgeir, himself a pagan priest, took a day and a night apart, then ruled that all should be baptised, because to tear the law would tear the peace.
stations.limit: Ari wrote about a century and a quarter later. The famous story of Thorgeir throwing his idols into a waterfall is not in him: it appears to be a nineteenth-century addition.

stations.name: Norway
stations.head: Two kings named Olaf.
stations.text: Olaf Tryggvason pressed the faith by every means from 995. After he fell in 1000 the old ways returned in part. Olaf Haraldsson pressed it again, and died in battle at Stiklestad in 1030.
stations.limit: The fullest accounts are sagas written about two centuries on, with a saint to honour. The figure given for when they were written is a round one.

stations.name: Sweden
stations.head: Over two hundred years on, a temple is still described.
stations.text: Ansgar first reached Birka in the 830s. About 1075 Adam of Bremen still describes a great temple at Uppsala, with Thor, Odin and Freyr enthroned. Sweden's archdiocese came only in 1164.
stations.limit: Adam wrote from Bremen, on reports and with a cause. Whether a temple existed as he describes it is now questioned. His account shows what a churchman thought was still there.

stations.name: Prussia
stations.head: A crusade for a mission.
stations.text: A bishop's preaching failed, and the Teutonic Knights were invited in. Half a century of war followed. The people who were conquered did not write their own account.
stations.limit: Peter of Dusburg, the Order's chronicler, wrote about 1326 for the Order. The Prussian language later died out and there is no account from the other side.

missionStand.head: Where this site stands
missionStand.text: This site holds with the Baptist Faith and Message 2000 that “God alone is Lord of the conscience”, and that baptism is the immersion of a believer. So it reads a ruler's baptism and a forced one as history, and does not count either as a people's coming to faith. It says so of Charlemagne and of Harald, and it gives thanks for those who came preaching. Who among these people truly believed is not something the record can show, in either direction.

rounds.why: A claim in a letter, with nothing yet tested.
rounds.limit: Gelasius wrote as one party. The letter does not say how the emperor took it.
rounds.head: Two powers named.
rounds.text: “There are two powers, august Emperor, by which this world is chiefly ruled”: the priests' authority and the royal power. He adds that the priests' is the more weighty. This is a claim and not yet a contest.

rounds.why: Each side gained what it could not get alone.
rounds.limit: Read through a reference article and not the chroniclers.
rounds.head: Each makes the other.
rounds.text: Pippin takes the Frankish crown in 751, and popes back the change. In 756 he hands the pope lands in central Italy. The pope gets territory and a protector, and the king gets a blessing on a new dynasty.

rounds.why: Both readings of that crown stayed open.
rounds.limit: Einhard admired the king and wrote after his death. The king's dislike is his report, and cannot be tested.
rounds.head: Who crowned whom?
rounds.text: On Christmas Day at Rome the pope crowns Charlemagne emperor. Einhard says the king so disliked the titles “that he would not have set foot in the Church” had he foreseen the pope's design. A crown from a pope could later be read either way.

rounds.why: A king's army settled who was pope.
rounds.limit: Read through a reference article and not the synod's own record.
rounds.head: An emperor sorts out the popes.
rounds.text: Three men claim the papacy. King Henry III crosses the Alps with an army, calls a synod at Sutri and has a German bishop made pope, who then crowns him. The reformers who later opposed kings first rose with a king's help.

rounds.why: A king came as a penitent, to a pope's terms.
rounds.limit: Some read it as Henry's clever escape, since being absolved undercut the princes against him. See the record for that pair.
rounds.head: A king at the gate.
rounds.text: Gregory excommunicates and deposes Henry, and German princes turn on him. In January 1077 Henry waits for three days at Canossa as a penitent, and is absolved. In the picture beside this panel, he kneels to ask Matilda of Tuscany and Abbot Hugh to speak for him.

rounds.why: The king held the city, and the pope left with his rescuers.
rounds.limit: Gregory never gave up the claim, and popes after him kept it.
rounds.head: A king at the walls.
rounds.text: Seven years on, Henry enters Rome, an opposing pope crowns him, and Gregory dies at Salerno. Canossa is the scene people remember. It was not the end of the story.

rounds.why: Each side kept something it could name as the point.
rounds.limit: It settled terms for the Empire. England had made its own arrangement earlier.
rounds.head: Ring and staff for one, sceptre for the other.
rounds.text: The emperor surrenders “all investiture through ring and staff”, the signs of a bishop's spiritual office. The pope grants that elections in Germany “shall take place in thy presence” and that the bishop takes his lands by the sceptre. Both can claim the day.

rounds.why: The king gave up on paper what he had fought for.
rounds.limit: How far Avranches changed daily practice in English courts is not settled by what this study read.
rounds.head: A murder changes the terms.
rounds.text: Henry's rules of 1164 are opposed by his archbishop, who is killed in 1170. At Avranches in 1172 the king accepts appeals to Rome. A dead archbishop did what a living one could not.

rounds.why: A king formally held his kingdom from the pope.
rounds.limit: It was John's own bargain, and it served him.
rounds.head: A kingdom held from Rome.
rounds.text: After years under interdict, and fearing a French invasion, John surrenders England to the papacy and takes it back for a yearly payment of 1,000 marks. It was also a shrewd move: it gave him a powerful ally against his enemies.

rounds.why: The king's men laid hands on the pope, and he died that year.
rounds.limit: Townspeople freed him within days, and this study does not say the bull alone caused the attack.
rounds.head: The highest claim, and a palace stormed.
rounds.text: Unam Sanctam reads “two swords” from the disciples' words in Luke and puts both in the church's power. A year later the king's men hold the pope captive at Anagni.

rounds.why: French popes, close to the French crown.
rounds.limit: The town was not French, and how far those popes were the crown's men is argued.
rounds.head: The court moves north.
rounds.text: The papal court settles at Avignon, under seven French popes. The town was in the Kingdom of Arles, inside the Empire, and bought by the pope in 1348, so this was not simply captivity. The tilt here is this study's closest and least certain call.

roundsNote: Each tilt is this study's judgement of who came out ahead in that one event, not a measurement. The same event was read in opposite ways at the time and since. Nothing here adds up to a score.

powersStand.head: Where this site stands
powersStand.text: Scripture tells believers to give to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's, and the disciples' “two swords” answer a moment on the road to the garden and name no office. The Baptist Faith and Message 2000 holds that church and state are to be separate, and calls “A free church in a free state” the Christian ideal, so this site stands with neither pope nor king in these contests. Unam Sanctam makes subjection to the pope necessary for salvation. Baptists do not hold that: Scripture names Christ as the head of the church. Catholic teaching on the papacy is reported here as its own.

article.cite: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica, First Part, question 2, article 3, about 1265 to 1274
article.note: Aquinas's words, in the English Dominican translation. Shortened where three dots show. Shown for how the argument is built: this site's own ground for belief in God is Scripture, and it does not rest on his five ways.

parts.name: Whether God exists?
parts.does: It asks as an open question something the writer believes with his whole life. The form requires it.

parts.name: There is evil
parts.text: It seems that God does not exist; because if one of two contraries be infinite, the other would be altogether destroyed … there is evil in the world. Therefore God does not exist.
parts.does: The other side goes first, in a strong short form, in his own words.

parts.name: Nature is enough
parts.text: … it seems that everything we see in the world can be accounted for by other principles, supposing God did not exist.
parts.does: A second, different objection. Written about 750 years ago, it still reads as current.

parts.name: “I am Who am”
parts.text: It is said in the person of God: “I am Who am.” (Exodus 3:14)
parts.does: One authority against the objections, here Scripture. It does not yet argue. It shows there is a question to resolve.

parts.name: Five ways
parts.text: The existence of God can be proved in five ways.
parts.does: The master's own decision, the body of the article: from motion, from causes, from what need not exist, from degrees of good, and from the order of things.

parts.name: Good out of evil
parts.text: As Augustine says … “He would not allow any evil to exist in His works, unless His omnipotence and goodness were such as to bring good even out of evil.”
parts.does: He comes back to the first objection and answers that one, by name.

parts.name: Nature has a cause
parts.text: Since nature works for a determinate end under the direction of a higher agent, whatever is done by nature must needs be traced back to God, as to its first cause.
parts.does: He comes back to the second. No objection may be left standing unanswered.

abelard.text: The form did not begin with Aquinas. About 1120 Peter Abelard, in a book called Sic et Non (Yes and No), set authorities side by side where they seemed to disagree, on purpose, for the student to work through.
abelard.quote: through doubting we come to questioning and through questions we perceive the truth

ladder.note: From the statutes of 1215. The ages are the minimums the statute names. What it does not name, such as the age a boy began, is this study's working back, hatched on the drawing.

steps.name: Listen in arts
steps.text: “He is to listen in arts at least six years”: so about fourteen, if he reached lecturing at the earliest age.

steps.name: Lecture in arts
steps.text: “No one is to lecture at Paris in arts before he is twenty years old”, and he promises at least two years of it.

steps.name: Study theology
steps.text: “Not unless he has studied at least eight years”, five of them listening: the statute fixes the length and the age at the end, so the start is worked back.

steps.name: Lecture in theology
steps.text: “no one shall lecture at Paris before he is thirty-five years old”. The bar runs on past the edge because there is no upper limit.

schools.name: Bologna
schools.note: 1088 was fixed by a nineteenth-century committee. The student guilds that made it a university appear in the late 1100s.

schools.name: Paris
schools.note: It grew out of the cathedral school. The 1215 statutes on this page are among its first.

schools.name: Oxford
schools.note: Growth is linked to Henry II barring English students from Paris. The story of Alfred's founding is a later invention.

schools.name: Cambridge
schools.note: Dated from scholars leaving Oxford after a dispute.

schoolStand.head: Where this site stands
schoolStand.text: The Baptist Faith and Message 2000 treats sound learning as part of the Christian inheritance, held under “the pre-eminence of Jesus Christ” and the authority of Scripture. So this site can admire a method that hears the other side first, and read Aquinas for it. It does not take on the Roman Catholic teaching his work carries.

parish.note: An illustrative plan, not one particular church. It stands for a village church in the Latin West after about 1200. Many were smaller, and nearly all of them changed.

stations.name: The churchyard
stations.rule: If you did not confess yearly and receive at Easter, you were “cut off from the Church … during life and deprived of Christian burial in death”. Canon 21, 1215.
stations.record: Burial in this ground was something the church could withhold, and the council used it.
stations.limit: Canons state the penalty. They do not say how often a priest refused a grave, and this study found no count.

stations.name: The church door
stations.rule: Marriages “must be announced publicly in the churches by the priests”, and secret marriages are forbidden. Canon 51, 1215.
stations.record: The canon says it is extending “the particular custom that prevails in some” places to the rest. So the banns began as a local habit.
stations.limit: The canon forbids secret marriages but this page has not read the church-court records that show how many went on. Those courts are located, not read.

stations.name: The font
stations.rule: The chrism and the Eucharist are to be kept “in properly protected places provided with locks and keys”. Canon 20, 1215. Canon 1 says baptism is for “children and adults” alike and that anyone may give it in the right form.
stations.record: The canon names no age. This study takes infant baptism to be the ordinary practice of the time, which “children and adults” allows and does not state. So a whole parish could be baptised without those baptised being asked.
stations.limit: Canon 20 names the oil, not the water, and locks on fonts are a later English detail this study could not confirm. How soon after birth, parish by parish, is not something this study read.
stations.stand: Baptists hold that baptism is the immersion of a believer, a person who has personally trusted Christ, and find no infant baptism in the New Testament. Scripture pictures it as burial and rising with Christ, and the command is to baptize disciples. That is this site's view. The practice here is reported as the medieval church's.

stations.name: The nave wall
stations.rule: “What writing presents to readers, this a picture presents to the unlearned who behold.” Pope Gregory I, about 600, telling a bishop of Marseilles who had broken images not to.
stations.record: Gregory praises him for forbidding the images to be adored, and blames him for breaking them. So a picture was to teach, not to receive worship. The letter assumes people who could not read. How many stood in any one nave, it does not say.
stations.limit: This is what a pope said a picture was for. What a villager took from a painted wall, nobody wrote down. Most wall paintings that survive are later than this page's period.

stations.name: The chancel arch
stations.rule: Bishops must “diligently prepare and instruct” those they ordain, canon 27, and provide men to preach when they cannot, canon 10. Both 1215. In 1281 Pecham's priests were told to explain the faith in the people's tongue four times a year.
stations.record: In 1222 Simon at Sonning could read the Mass and not construe it. Latin prayers ran beyond this arch, and any teaching in English or French had to come from the priest in front of it.
stations.limit: This is one examined priest, and his ignorance is why he was recorded. What ordinary sermons said rarely survives from parish level before 1350.

stations.name: The altar
stations.rule: At least once a year, at Easter, receive. Canon 21. Canon 1 defines the bread as “changed (transsubstantiatio) by divine power into the body”, and says only a duly ordained priest can effect it.
stations.record: A small box such as the one pictured here held the bread. The rule sets a floor of once a year. This study infers that the council did not expect much more of many people, and cannot say how many.
stations.limit: A minimum is not a measure. Some surely came more often, and some never came. No parish register of communions survives from this period for this study to count.
stations.stand: Baptists hold the Lord's Supper to be a symbolic act of remembrance, and that there is “one mediator between God and men”, Christ. That is this site's view. The teaching here is reported as the council's.

claims.claim: “Medieval Christians thought the earth was flat.”
claims.head: The schoolbook said round. The story is modern.
claims.evidence: Aquinas, in the first article of the Summa, uses as his ordinary example that astronomer and physicist can both prove “that the earth, for instance, is round”. He is not arguing it: he assumes his reader agrees. Historian Jeffrey Burton Russell traces the flat-earth story largely to writers of the 1800s.
claims.inference: Among educated people the claim is false. Those who repeat it are repeating a nineteenth-century story about the Middle Ages.
claims.limit: Aquinas speaks for the schools. What a ploughman thought about the shape of the earth is not recorded either way.

options.text: That learned readers could take a round earth for granted.
options.why: He uses it as a plain example in passing. It shows what he expected his readers to accept.

options.text: That every person in Europe knew the earth was round.
options.why: One master's example cannot speak for villagers, and no record of their views was kept.

options.text: That the church had defined the earth's shape as doctrine.
options.why: An example in a discussion of how sciences differ is not a definition by anyone.

claims.claim: “The medieval church forbade ordinary people to read the Bible.”
claims.head: Some bishops did. No ruling for all has been found.
claims.evidence: The council of the province of Toulouse in 1229 said: “We prohibit also that the laity should be permitted to have the books of the Old and New Testaments”, excepting the Psalter and service books, and forbade translations most strictly. A synod at Tarragona in 1234, following a decree of King James I of Aragon, ordered translations brought in to be burned. A synod at Béziers in 1246 denied the laity theological books in Latin and the common tongue. These came amid conflict with the Cathars and Waldensians. Innocent III in 1199 banned secret meetings over the Bible at Metz while saying the desire to study it was not to blame.
claims.inference: The popular claim is too wide, and “it never happened” is false as well. Real bans existed, were local, and were aimed at dissent. Far more people were kept from the Bible by the cost of a book and not knowing how to read it than by any ruling. This is a matter this page can only begin: the later English story belongs to the Reformation outline.
claims.limit: This study read Toulouse through reference works and not the Latin. A statement that no general ban exists rests on what scholars report. It cannot be proved by this study's own search.

test.question: A friend says “the Council of Toulouse proves the church banned the Bible for everyone.” What can the evidence say?

options.text: A real ban, in one province, in a war with dissent. It does not reach everyone.
options.why: Toulouse is a provincial council. A council at Béziers in 1233 reused other parts of its rulings and left this one out, though a synod there in 1246 went its own way against lay books.

options.text: The ban never existed: this is a Protestant invention.
options.why: The canon is real, and the same record shows Tarragona burning translations.

options.text: Yes. A council's word bound the whole Western church.
options.why: A provincial council binds its province. That is the difference this claim blurs.

claims.head: He claimed much. Kings answered.
claims.evidence: The Dictates say he may depose emperors, and Unam Sanctam says every creature must be subject to him. Henry IV took Rome in 1084, and Philip IV's men seized Boniface in 1303. John did hand England to Innocent III in 1213, which is the claim's best case, and it was John's own bargain.
claims.inference: The papacy was a real power, able to shake kings. It did not govern Europe. It could be defied, and the strongest claims came when contested.
claims.limit: This page follows the biggest quarrels. In ordinary years, popes and kings worked together on bishops and taxes, and those years leave less drama and need another study.

test.question: What does the sentence in Unam Sanctam, by itself, establish?

options.why: A document is first of all evidence of what its writer said.

options.text: That Europe's kings obeyed the pope.
options.why: Anagni, one year later, is the answer. A claim is not its own proof.

options.text: That no one took the claim seriously.
options.why: The quarrel ran wider than this one bull, but Philip's side plainly did not wave the claim away.

claims.claim: “It was an age when everyone believed.”
claims.head: Baptism was the norm. Belief is another question.
claims.evidence: Canon 21 sets a penalty for not confessing yearly. Bede's Rædwald kept two altars, and Iceland's law allowed private sacrifice at first. On the other side stand costly lives such as that of Boniface, killed in his old age on mission.
claims.inference: This study takes the medieval rite of baptism to have been the norm among Latin Christians by 1350, with Jews, Muslims in Spain and Sicily, and pagans in Lithuania outside it. That is a fact about an institution. What each person believed cannot be read off it, whether to praise them or to dismiss them.
claims.limit: The record favours rulers, clergy and offenders. An ordinary believing villager, or an ordinary doubting one, rarely leaves a word.

test.question: A canon threatens those who do not confess each year. What follows?

options.text: Some people may not have been doing it, and the rule-makers cared that they should.
options.why: A rule points to a concern. How large the problem was, it does not say.
A failure to confess is not a measure of belief, and the canon gives no number.

options.text: Everyone obeyed, because a council had spoken.
options.why: Rule and practice are the difference this page keeps asking about.

confusedWords.note: A canon shows what its makers wanted. Only other evidence shows what followed.

On this page “baptised” reports the medieval rite. It could be counted, ordered or forced. Faith cannot be, and a record of the first is not a record of the second. The site's own view of baptism is in the panels that say so.
A document claiming authority is evidence for the claim. Power shows when someone tests it.

confusedWords.word: A general and a provincial council
confusedWords.note: A general council spoke for the Western church in that age's reckoning. A provincial one bound its own province.
A rule repeated may mean it was being broken, or only that it was being kept in view. Repetition alone cannot tell which.
Universities mostly grew. A “founding” date is often a later choice among several true events.
In these records “the church” usually means the institution and its officers. The parishioners in the nave left almost no writing.

reach: This is a selection: eleven pairs, eleven places and eleven contests, chosen to reach each part of the entry for this study and to show the gap at its plainest. It is not a census or a narrative history. The pairs were picked because they show a gap, so they cannot measure how often rules were kept.

Eastern Europe and the Mediterranean are thin. Spain, Ireland, Italian towns, Hungary, Bohemia and Lithuania are named lightly or not at all. Women appear here far less than they did in that church: abbesses, Matilda and the women in the nave deserve more than this page gives.

Much of the throne and mission detail comes through reference articles and not the chroniclers. Each source below says so. The canons, statutes, Bede, Aquinas, Gregory and the visitation records were read directly in the English named, and Alcuin's sentence in Latin.
Ranges on the charts run from a source's stated years. Where a range is this study's own, the page says so.
